title: Rep Playbook: Opponent Tactics & Rebuttals vs LLM API Providers
content:
TL;DR
Quick, tactical playbook for AEs and SDRs to handle common competitor claims from LLM API vendors. Focus areas: price/latency claims, private deployment/VM options, SLA/uptime promises, model freshness, and operational observability. Use the questions and rebuttals below to surface gaps, then move to Redwood differentiators (predictable economics, unified runtime across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, rollout controls).

Audience
- AEs running deal cycles with mid-market/enterprise infra or product teams.
- SEs prepping demos and POCs.

How to use this doc
- Read top section for quick rebuttal lines.
- Use competitor snapshots during discovery to map decision criteria.
- Follow the demo checklist at the end for probing gaps (SLOs, failover, cost controls).

Competitor snapshots (quick heuristics)
1) CloudSimple APIs (pricing-first players)
- What they say: "Cheaper per-token + simple dev experience"
- Typical limitation: Hidden tail costs (no TTL for KV cache), weak batching knobs, limited private deployment (only VPC peering).
- Ask: "How do you handle KV cache invalidation and cross-request caching? What's the billing delta when requests drop into microsecond latency targets?"
- Rebuttal line: "Cheaper per-token on paper often becomes more expensive once you add retries, prefix storage, and lack of batching controls. Redwood shows token-level cost and token-level latency; customers like predictable per-route control."

2) FastServe Cloud (latency-first edge claims)
- What they say: "Lowest end-to-end latency with edge nodes"
- Typical limitation: Model variants inconsistent across regions, limited model catalog, no canary rollout support for model updates.
- Ask: "How do you guarantee model parity between edge regions and your control plane? Can you fallback to a smaller model if the primary node is saturated?"
- Rebuttal line: "Edge speed is great until model parity and fallback policies cause behavioral drift. Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible variants to avoid outages and regressions during peak."

3) OnPremVendor (self-host focused)
- What they say: "Full data sovereignty — run everything on-prem"
- Typical limitation: Heavy ops lift, no out-of-the-box observability, inconsistent kernel + quantization support across hardware.
- Ask: "How long does a new model onboarding take and who owns kernel optimization work? What visibility do you give into token-level costs?"
- Rebuttal line: "On-prem control is valid for regulated workloads, but most teams prefer a hybrid option: private control plane + managed inference (Redwood Private). We handle kernel selection, autoscaling, and observability so internal teams don't become 24/7 ops owners."

Top objection categories and scripts
1) "Your price is higher"
- Rebuttal bullets: Ask what they mean by price (list price vs delivered unit cost after retries, caching, batching). Offer to run a quick 1-hour cost profile: sample traffic + 5k requests to show savings from batching/prefix-cache. Emphasize predictable committed capacity for Dedicated that caps unit price.
- Script: "Totally fair — price matters. Can we run a short traffic replay so I can show you exact unit economics and how our batching/caching drops their effective cost?"

2) "We can't move to a hosted vendor for compliance"
- Rebuttal bullets: Surface private options early: private control plane, VPC connectors, on-prem package. Ask about KMS/HSM requirements and audit log needs.
- Script: "We support VPC and on-prem installs with KMS integrations — can you share the specific audit/KMS requirements so I can confirm fit?"

3) "We just need simple API access"
- Rebuttal bullets: Simple API is table stakes. Push for what they care about next — SLOs, cost visibility, rollout guarantees, and model quality guardrails.
- Script: "Agree — the API is easy. What matters for your team in production: predictable latency, cost, or controlled model updates?"

Traps to call out in discovery (questions to expose weak spots)
- "How do you handle sudden traffic spikes — do you have graceful degradation/fallback policies or do requests get queued and errors spike?"
- "Show me a token-level cost breakdown for a mock route of 100k tokens/day — where do savings come from?"
- "When you upgrade a model, what rollback vectors do you have if behavior regresses against our eval suite?"
- "Do you provide per-prompt routing policy controls (by user, path, region)?"

Redwood talking points (concise)
- Unified runtime across Hosted / Dedicated / Private — same API and tooling.
- Predictable economics: batching, KV-prefix caching, quantization recommendations.
- Rollouts & reliability: canaries, A/B, auto-fallback to compatible variants.
- Observability: token-level cost, per-route latency, integration with tracing.
- Enterprise controls: KMS/HSM, audit logs, dedicated GPU pools with SLAs.

Proof points & quick evidence to cite
- "We ran a customer POC that reduced per-token cost by ~28% after enabling prefix cache + dynamic batching — we can share replayed traces (GIT: benchmark-results#482)."
- "Dedicated customers typically see 10–20% lower latencies at 99th percentile after kernel tuning on our runtime."
- "We support KMS integrations and we have an on-prem appliance offering; recent contract with a fintech customer included HSM provisioning and SOC2 artifacts."

Demo / POC checklist for SEs (what to show live)
- Start with baseline: call competitor’s public endpoint (if allowed) vs Redwood to show latency and token cost for a 3-turn chat replay.
- Turn on prefix caching and show token reduction for repeated prefixes.
- Show route-level cost/latency dashboard, then simulate model rollout and execute rollback.
- If private/on-prem: show the control plane vs local execution parity.

Closing plays (pressure points)
- For price objections: offer a limited-time committed Dedicated trial with transparent benchmarking and a migration SLA.
- For compliance: offer an architecture review (free) with infra + security to map gaps and a proposed rollout timeline.
- For reliability-focused buyers: propose a 30-day canary with a staged rollback plan and incident runbook alignment.

Notes to self / follow-ups
- Sync with Benchmarking team on latest quantization bench (Miguel) — add new numbers to this doc (JIRA GTM-842).
- Draft a 1-pager cost-replay template for AEs to attach to proposals.

Appendix: quick rebuttal cheat-sheet (one-liners)
- "Lowest price claim? Let’s look at delivered unit cost including retries, cache misses, and tail queuing."
- "Edge latency claim? Great — who owns model parity and rollouts across regions?"
- "On-prem only? Fine — do you want to own kernel optimization forever or have a hybrid option to reduce ops debt?"

End — keep this lean. Update after next bench run and after field feedback from two deals this quarter.
